extracted.intended_audience: IP and regulatory attorneys, in-house counsel, and industry stakeholders involved in FDA drug approvals, generics, and Hatch‑Waxman litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of statutory and regulatory requirements, timing rules, and litigation triggers under the Hatch‑Waxman Act governing NDAs, ANDAs, 505(b)(2) applications, Orange Book listings, Paragraph certifications, 30‑month stays, and 180‑day exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: NDA substantive requirements & patent listing
rubrics_metrics.description: An NDA must be supported by studies supporting the subject drug's safety and efficacy; drug efficacy studies must include adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations. NDA applicants must submit to FDA any patents that claim the drug itself or a method of using the drug for which approval is sought (for listing in the Orange Book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products approved through NDAs are often the reference listed drugs (RLDs) relied upon by ANDA applicants. NDA sponsors are required to list patents covering a drug substance, drug product, or an approved method of use; product-by-process patents where the product claimed is novel; and drug delivery system patents where the patent recites a drug substance or product.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANDA substantive requirements (bioequivalence and labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ANDA generally must seek approval for the same conditions of use and have the same labeling as the RLD and need not contain new clinical studies. Instead, an ANDA must include data showing that the proposed drug is bioequivalent to the RLD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bioequivalence means the ANDA product and RLD are pharmaceutically equivalent (same active ingredient(s), dosage form, strength, quality, purity, and identity) and that their rates and extents of absorption do not differ significantly under experimental conditions. Certain differences can be reconciled with a suitability petition to FDA if clinical trials are not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 505(b)(2) hybrid pathway requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A 505(b)(2) application must contain safety and efficacy data but may rely on studies not conducted by the applicant and for which the applicant has not obtained a right of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 505(b)(2)s are used when the proposed drug differs from an RLD (new dosage form, different strength, different chemical form). This pathway is generally unavailable where the applicant seeks approval for a pharmaceutical equivalent of an RLD (in that case an ANDA is required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orange Book listing prohibitions and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: FDA regulations prohibit the listing of patents claiming packaging, metabolites, intermediates, unapproved methods of use, or methods of manufacturing. The Orange Book lists drugs approved to be marketed in the United States and the patents sponsors submit for listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orange Book listings should include patents covering drug substance, drug product, approved methods of use, product-by-process patents where product claimed is novel, and certain drug delivery system patents. FDA does not currently review the propriety of patents submitted for listing, which has led to disputes over improper listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial act of infringement and notice letter requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hatch‑Waxman Act classifies the act of filing an ANDA or 505(b)(2) application as an artificial act of infringement for purposes of establishing jurisdiction, and an ANDA applicant must send a notice letter to the NDA holder and all owners of Orange Book patents claiming the RLD or uses for which approval is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Notice Letter must include a detailed statement of the factual and legal bases for the applicant's opinion that the listed patent will not be infringed and/or is invalid or unenforceable, and may contain an offer of confidential access to the applicant's ANDA if non‑infringement is asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph I–IV certifications
rubrics_metrics.description: An ANDA must contain one of four certifications to each Orange Book patent: Paragraph I – no patent information filed; Paragraph II – the listed patent has expired; Paragraph III – sponsor does not intend to market until after patent expiration; Paragraph IV – the ANDA product will not infringe or the listed patent is invalid or unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A filer referencing a method of use patent can alternatively file a section viii statement (see separate criterion). Paragraph IV filings trigger Notice Letter, potential litigation, and the possibility of a 30‑month stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section viii statements and skinny labels (carve‑outs)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ANDA filer can submit a section viii statement asserting that the listed method patent does not claim a use for which the applicant seeks approval; this must be accompanied by a 'skinny label' that carves out the patented use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A section viii statement avoids Paragraph IV certification, Notice Letter, litigation trigger, and any 30‑month stay associated with the method-of-use patent. FDA analyzes carve‑outs case‑by‑case and may require a Paragraph III/IV or label revision if a carve‑out is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split certifications for mixed patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent contains both method-of-use claims and claims to drug products or substances, an ANDA applicant can submit a split certification: section viii for method claims and Paragraph III or IV certifications for product/substance claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split certifications allow an applicant to carve out patented uses while still certifying to product claims that may require litigation triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for FDA acceptance and timing of Notice Letters
rubrics_metrics.description: After an applicant submits an ANDA, FDA has 60 days to determine whether it will be accepted for filing. Within 20 days of FDA notifying the ANDA sponsor that the ANDA has been accepted for filing, the applicant must send any required Notice Letter and provide documentation of receipt of each Notice Letter to FDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date of notice receipt (when multiple recipients, the latest-receiving party) affects timing for litigation and 30‑month stay start dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-listed patents and certification obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the USPTO issues a relevant patent after an NDA has been submitted to or approved by FDA, the NDA holder has 30 days after issuance to submit the patent to FDA for Orange Book listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the NDA holder submits within 30 days, applicants with unapproved ANDAs on file and subsequent filers must file a certification to the late-listed patent. If the NDA holder does not submit within 30 days, only applicants that have not yet filed their ANDAs must certify; applicants with an ANDA already on file need not certify (though there may be strategic reasons to do so).

rubrics_metrics.name: 30‑month stay of FDA approval (trigger and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hatch‑Waxman Act provides an automatic 30‑month stay of FDA approval of generics pending litigation if the NDA holder brings an infringement suit within 45 days of receiving an applicant's Notice Letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the NDA holder fails to file suit during the 45‑day window, it is not entitled to a 30‑month stay. The 30‑month stay only blocks final FDA approval (FDA can tentatively approve during the stay). Under the MMA, a 30‑month stay is not available for patents listed after an ANDA or 505(b)(2) was submitted, with some limited exceptions (e.g., conversion of a Paragraph III to IV). Courts may extend or reduce the stay for parties' failure to reasonably cooperate in expediting litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCE / NCE‑1 special timing impact on stay
rubrics_metrics.description: For products deemed New Chemical Entities (NCE), the 30‑month stay may extend beyond 30 months (approximately 40 months or 7.5 years from first approval) to allow the NDA holder to obtain the full benefit of five‑year NCE regulatory exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ANDA with a Paragraph IV certification may be filed one year before the five‑year period expires (NCE‑1 date); timing rules for stays differ in that context so Congress provided a longer stay to preserve NCE exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination and modification of the 30‑month stay
rubrics_metrics.description: A 30‑month stay terminates on the date a district court enters a judgment of non‑infringement, invalidity, or unenforceability; or enters a settlement order or consent decree containing such a finding. It can also terminate if the patentee waives its rights to a stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a court does not render a decision within 30 months, a patentee may seek a preliminary injunction or other order to extend the stay. Successful appeals affecting infringement or invalidity similarly terminate the stay when the appeals court enters judgment or settlement order. Courts can extend or reduce the stay where litigation conduct impedes expedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delisting counterclaims and enforcement scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there is no private right of action to delist an improperly listed patent, the 2003 Medicare Modernization Act (MMA) allows an ANDA applicant to assert a delisting counterclaim against the owner of an improperly listed patent in any litigation that results from such patent listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC has announced increased scrutiny of improperly listed patents, sent warning letters to manufacturers, and filed amici briefs in patent cases highlighting anticompetitive effects. An ANDA applicant can also bring a delisting counterclaim if an Orange Book use code is overly broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: 180‑day first‑filer exclusivity entitlement and forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: The first applicant(s) to file a 'substantially complete' ANDA with a Paragraph IV certification to any patent listed for the RLD can obtain a 180‑day exclusivity period during which subsequent ANDAs for the same product will not be approved; exclusivity can be shared among multiple first‑day filers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial marketing of a first‑filer's ANDA product starts the 180‑day period (any first filer who markets can trigger start when exclusivity is shared). Under the MMA, a first filer can forfeit exclusivity for events intended to prevent bottlenecking: failure to market or obtain tentative approval within specified time; withdrawal of ANDA; amendment/withdrawal of Paragraph IV; entering into anticompetitive agreements as found by FTC or appeals court; or if all patents certified to have expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA's non‑review of listing propriety and enforcement risk
rubrics_metrics.description: FDA does not currently review the propriety of patents submitted for Orange Book listing, which has permitted allegations of improper listings aimed at delaying generic entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because FDA does not screen listings, other mechanisms (MMA delisting counterclaims, FTC scrutiny and enforcement, antitrust challenges) are avenues to address improper listings.
